name: Duration Field
summary: Accepts 90m, 1:30, 2h30 or 1d 4h, shows what it understood in three forms, and steps by hour, minute or second from the keyboard.

attempts.prompt: Build an input that accepts a duration like 2h30m.
attempts.problem: Matched a single strict pattern, so "2h30m" worked and "2h 30m", "90m", "1:30" and "2h30" were all rejected. Every one of those is how someone actually types a duration, so the field was correct and unusable. It also gave no feedback about what it had parsed, leaving the user to guess whether "1h" had been understood as one hour or one minute.

attempts.prompt: Accept more formats and show the parsed result.
attempts.problem: Accepted more formats but treated a bare number after a unit as the same unit, so "2h30" parsed as thirty-two hours rather than two and a half. It also reformatted the input on every keystroke, so typing "1" toward "1h" immediately rewrote the field to "1m" and moved the caret.

finalPrompt:
Build a duration input in plain HTML, CSS and vanilla JavaScript, no dependencies. The parser is the component.

Accept all of these and treat them as the same value where they are the same: "2h 30m", "2h30m", "2h30", "150m", "1:30", "1:30:00". Also accept days and seconds, long unit names, and decimal values.

The rule that makes it feel right: a bare number following a unit inherits the next smaller unit. "2h30" is two hours thirty minutes, "1d4" is one day four hours. A bare number with no preceding unit means minutes. Getting this wrong turns two and a half hours into thirty-two hours, which is the kind of error that reaches production.

Handle clock form separately and first — a colon means hours, minutes and optional seconds — because trying to fold it into the unit parser produces wrong answers for "1:30".

Echo what was understood in three forms at once: the normalised short form, the same duration in words, and the total in seconds. A duration field that does not show its interpretation makes the user run an experiment to find out.

Normalise the text only on blur. Validate on input, never rewrite mid-keystroke: a field that reformats while you type makes typing a two-part duration impossible.

Arrow Up and Down step by one minute, Shift by one hour, Alt by one second, and clamp at zero.

Mark unparseable input with aria-invalid and say plainly that it is not a duration yet, rather than blocking keystrokes.

Announce the interpretation through a role="status" region.

Colour comes only from CSS custom properties: var(--bg), var(--raised), var(--border), var(--text), var(--text-dim), var(--accent), var(--mono). No literal hex, rgb or hsl values.
why:
This component is a parser wearing an input, and the prompt that worked treats it that way: it spends its words on grammar rules and worked examples rather than on appearance.

The inherit-the-next-smaller-unit rule is the whole thing. It is how every human writes durations and it is not a rule a model will infer, because the obvious reading of a bare number is the previous unit. Giving two worked examples with their expected results left no room for a different interpretation.

Separating clock form and handling it first is a general parser lesson. Two grammars that overlap in their character set need separate passes in a defined order; folding them into one regex produces confident wrong answers rather than failures, which is worse.

And the same validate-on-input, normalise-on-blur split as the unit field. Two components, same fix, because the underlying mistake — treating validation and formatting as one step — is the default.
